title: Dangling Modifiers & Participle Traps: Why 'Walking in the Park, a Snake Bit Him' Is Dead Wrong
excerpt: Dangling participles sound innocent in conversation but are fatal in competitive exams. Learn how to anchor the subject of reference in 2 seconds.
content:
Have you ever encountered a sentence like: "Entering the room, the lights went out"? Who entered the room? The lights? Of course not! Yet the modifier points grammatically to 'the lights'. This is the classic Dangling Modifier / Unattached Participle trap.

The Logic of Participle Clauses

When an introductory participle phrase (starting with a V-ing or V3) opens a sentence, it borrows its grammatical subject from the noun immediately following the comma.

❌ Being a rainy day, I decided to stay indoors.
✅ It being a rainy day, I decided to stay indoors. (or: As it was a rainy day, I decided to stay indoors.)

Why was the first sentence wrong? Because without 'It', the subject for 'Being a rainy day' defaults to 'I', implying 'I was a rainy day'!
